articles.title: Xi, Putin, and Trump meeting concludes with vague commitments, but strong symbolism
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Chinese President Xi Jinping held the first ever trilateral summit of Russia, China, and the US on the sidelines of the ongoing Asia-Pacific Economic Council (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, November 19. The meeting, attended by Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, ended with a joint Declaration towards Peace with all three countries agreeing to find ways to work together on common issues including the need for reforms in the UN, global energy security, and rising nuclear risk. The declaration also talked about the principles of the operation of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and underlined the immunity for top state officials. The declaration emphasized that the reforms in the UN are necessary for it to make effective interventions to issues of global concern and to fulfill its mandate of preserving global peace and security. The point was an indirect reflection on recent failures of the UN to make any meaningful intervention in the global conflicts particularly its failure to prevent the Israel’s genocide in Gaza, the war in Ukraine and the US-Israeli war on Iran. All three countries also agreed that they should work together to reduce the risks of a nuclear war breaking out. They underlined the need to conduct dialogue for reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. The three heads of states also agreed it was necessary to maintain the global flow of energy and to minimize the disruptions to global energy supply chains even during conflict and to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum to ease constraints on general production and prices. Thycydides trap is not destiny During his speech in the summit, hinting towards recent conflicts, Xi pointed out that there must be peace among major countries in the world in order to maintain global stability and to avoid chaos. Asking for a more friendly and trust based relations between the great power Xi denounced the conventional notions of great power rivalry repeating that the so-called “Thucydides Trap is by no means a destiny.” Thycydides, an ancient Greek historian, is often quoted to describe conflicts and rivalries between a rising power and an established one. As major countries and the permanent members of the UN Security Council China, Russia and the US must work together to meet global challenges and jointly uphold world peace and stability. They together can make greater contributions to the progress of humanity, Xi argued. Xi recalled how China, Russia and the US have worked together in the past to save the world from fascism during the Second World War claiming the same coordination is required now to “steadfastly safeguard the postwar international order, uphold the purposes and principles of the UN charter, and defend the hard-won outcomes.” Xi proposed a four point code of conduct for the great powers to work together; mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation and dialogue and consultation. For working together it is necessary that all the countries respect each other’s social structure and distinctive development paths adopted without trying to impose each other’s preferences over the other, Xi underlined. He also emphasized the UN principles of respecting each others’ sovereignty, territorial integrity and non-interference in domestic affairs as fundamental for good relations. “On major sensitive issues concerning one another, it is important to communicate in advance, try to see things from one another’s perspective, act with caution, and in particular, not to challenge the red lines of one another,” Xinhua reported Xi saying. Pointing towards the rising risks of nuclear conflicts and its possible impact on the existence of humanity, Xi talked about the need to push for complete nuclear disarmament. “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Domcleas that hangs over humanity, should be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons,” the Chinese leader said. Greater communication and coordination Indirectly referring to the impacts of US policies on global trade, Xi said that “decoupling and disruption of industrial and supply chains are not the ways to go” calling for stronger communication and coordination to “safeguard the security and stability of the global” markets. Both the US-Israeli war on Iran and Ukraine war have disrupted global supply chains of energy products. While Iran has restricted movements through the Strait of Hormuz in response to the US-Israeli war, Russia has been prevented from exporting freely due to sanctions and attacks on energy installations. Trump and Putin agreed with Xi’s call for a joint effort to push the countries to resolve their disputes through diplomatic channels with Putin emphasizing on “shared responsibilities” and calling for “proper resolution” of all “hotspot issues.” Trump claimed the three countries, the biggest military powers with the largest number of nuclear arsenals in the world, were “making history” by correcting a historical mistake of great powers not talking to each other.

articles.title: The daily reality of Israel’s mass extermination of life in Gaza
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: As Israel’s military aggression on the Gaza Strip enters its fourth year, devastating details continue to emerge regarding how every facet of daily life in Gaza has been engineered to maximize Palestinian casualties. In addition to fatalities caused directly by Israeli airstrikes, drones, artillery, and gunfire, the deprivation of basic necessities has been utilized as a weapon of war. This includes a lack of shelter during severe weather and acute shortages of food and essential supplies due to ongoing aid restrictions. Simultaneously, the healthcare system has been a primary target of military operations. Dr. Munir al-Bursh, director general of the Gaza Health Ministry, and Alaa Abu Odeh, the ministry’s director general of Engineering and Maintenance, addressed these issues in a recent discussion hosted by the Sword of Al-Quds Youth Forum. The systematic targeting of hospitals and medical infrastructure Dr. Munir explained how the systematic targeting of hospitals has dramatically driven up the death toll. He noted that Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, which was recently struck again, has been subjected to seven aerial assaults since October 2023. Read more: Israel resumes its lethal assaults on Gaza’s healthcare with new massacre at Nasser Medical complex By attacking hospitals, Israeli forces have not only targeted medical facilities, patients, and healthcare personnel, but have also inflicted mass killing on displaced civilians who sought refuge there, believing hospitals were protected under international law. Following the latest assault on Nasser Medical Complex , half of Gaza’s hospitals are now out of service. “Nineteen out of 38 hospitals are now non-operational,” Dr. Munir stated. Supporting networks for the healthcare system have also been devastated. Only 44 out of 116 generators remain functional. Meanwhile, out of 35 oxygen stations, only 12 are still operating. Severe damage to medical equipment has also impacted what Dr. Munir called the diagnostic capability at medical facilities. Vital machinery, including Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT) scanners, has been destroyed. “How is it reasonable for two million people in Gaza not to have access to even one MRI?” Al-Bursh asked. “We had six MRIs before the war; today, we have none.” He asserted. Dr. Munir clarified that an MRI at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City was destroyed by a missile, and he personally witnessed Israeli soldiers dismantling the gantry of a CT scanner at the Indonesian Hospital in the northern city of Beit Lahiya. The senior Palestinian health official said that in several instances, specialized technicians were brought by the Israeli military to remove specific components from medical devices. For his part, engineer Alaa Abu Odeh described the daily struggle to keep hospitals running amid severe shortages of water and electricity, which also threatens the desalination plants required for medical procedures such as dialysis. Regarding oxygen supply, he noted that only three or four oxygen-filling devices remain functional across Gaza. The sole functioning device at the Nasser Medical Complex – which supplied both the complex and surrounding local clinics and outpatients- was damaged in an assault earlier in November. Furthermore, a strict blockade on spare parts and industrial oil has crippled generators and ambulances. “Before the war, a liter of that oil cost $3,” Abu Odeh explained. “Today, a locally refined liter – with additives that can damage the longevity of the equipment – costs $1,200.” He also accused Israeli forces of fabricating media reports claiming they had repaired generators inside Nasser Medical Complex. “They brought in specialists to inflict irreparable damage on the machines and severed the fiber-optic cables connecting the CT scanner to its console,” Abu Odeh maintained. He further explained how Israeli warplanes struck the surgical building vertically from the rooftop – rather than horizontally through a window on the floor they claimed to have targeted – during the most recent assault on Nasser Medical Complex, maximizing structural devastation. “The airstrike completely destroyed the operating theaters, recovery rooms, and men’s surgery department, and partially damaged the laboratories, emergency room, and reception areas,” Abu Odeh reported. “Oxygen networks serving critical departments like the ICU were severed, and the building’s three elevators, water network, and sewage system were all knocked out of service,” he continued. The targeting of healthcare personnel Israel’s genocidal aggression on the Gaza Strip has resulted in significant loss of life and injury among medical personnel. Casualties and detentions Dr. Munir pointed out that at least 1,723 health workers have been killed and 362 others arrested since the genocide began, including Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, whose administrative detention was extended by another six months on Wednesday, November 18. Several detained medics have died in custody due to torture, including the late Dr. Adnan al-Bursh , who, according to testimonies cited by UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, was subjected to sexual violence in an Israeli prison. Workforce depletion “The number of doctors affiliated with Gaza’s Ministry of Health has dropped from 2,083 before the war to 1,300 – a loss of over 35% due to killings, detention, or forced displacement.” Dr. Munir declared. Suspicious role of NGOs in brain drain Dr. Munir criticized certain international organizations – primarily US-based – for undermining the Ministry of Health by poaching local staff with salaries of $4,000 to $6,000 per month. “These agencies operate on temporary contracts without providing comprehensive, sustainable care to the population. Israel permits their operations because they align with its political objectives,” he said. “While field hospitals have been established by such organizations, they cannot technically replace standard hospitals,” Al-Bursh emphasized. Indirect deaths, starvation, and the collapse of primary care The renowned Palestinian doctor indicated that for every person killed directly by a missile in Gaza, three have died indirectly due to the deprivation of medical care, food, and shelter. “Prior to the war, Gaza’s crude death rate stood at 6,000 annually; it has since quadrupled to 24,000.” Read more: Being bombed, starved to death, or killed while seeking food: Israel’s options for Palestinians in Gaza Starvation and aid traps Dr. Munir reported that over 466 people, including 157 children, have died of malnutrition. Adding that, more than 2,500 Palestinians – including 542 children – have been killed while attempting to access food at aid distribution centers. Blocked medical evacuations “Roughly 21,000 patients require urgent medical treatment abroad; more than 2,000 have died waiting for permission to leave Gaza,” he affirmed. Chronic diseases Dr. Munir suggested that with only 52 out of 159 primary care centers still operating and severe shortages of surgeons and basic supplies like insulin, chronic illnesses have become fatal. “The number of dialysis patients has dropped from 1,200 to 600, largely because patients died unable to access treatment. Meanwhile, the diabetic population has risen from 70,000 in 2022 to over 85,000, and hypertension cases have jumped from 110,000 to 130,000. Heart disease, tumors, and neurological conditions – exacerbated by displacement and environmental stress – are now the leading causes of death,” he said. Social and demographic devastation Al-Bursh characterized the situation as a “multi-faceted genocide,” encompassing health, social, environmental, and cultural destruction. Erased families and orphans Entire lineages have been wiped out, with 2,276 families completely erased from the civil registry, and another 2,800 families left with only a single survivor. The war has also left 24,000 women widowed and over 71,000 children orphaned. “When we talk about more than 71,000 orphans, one question comes to mind: who will take care of them?” Dr. Munir asked. The aggression has also wiped out 20% of Gaza’s labor force. Impact on births and children Annual births fell from 57,000 to 30,000 in 2023, recovering only partially to 50,000 in 2025. Dr. Munir contended that Israel banned the entry of folic acid to suppress Palestinian reproduction – which Israeli officials have historically viewed as a demographic threat – leading to an unprecedented spike in birth defects. Furthermore, over one million children are estimated to suffer from Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), though the destruction of all mental health facilities prevents full documentation. Withheld bodies and organ theft Dr. Munir also touched on the Israeli military’s treatment of deceased Palestinians. During prolonged sieges of hospitals like Al-Shifa and the Indonesian Hospital, staff were forced to bury the dead in makeshift mass graves on hospital grounds. “When Al-Shifa Hospital was besieged in 2023, Israeli forces exhumed bodies from the mass grave and confiscated them for about three months before returning them to Khan Younis, where they were reburied in another mass grave,” he said. Following an Israeli strike on a school sheltering families near the Indonesian Hospital, Dr. Munir visited the site and found classrooms converted into makeshift surgical rooms equipped with beds and bandages. “I didn’t understand what I had seen at first,” he recounted. “I pieced it together later when I saw similar setups near other hospitals, alongside reports that Israel had set a Guinness World Record for the largest gathering of kidney donors.” He stated that upon recovering certain bodies, medical staff observed incisions made by surgical saws, stitched with medical sutures, and cavities – where kidneys and other organs had been removed – stuffed with cotton and gauze. Medical officials have called for an international investigation into these findings, though no action has been taken. The collapse of infrastructure and lack of international support have also hindered dignified burials. Lack of morgues With no electricity or functioning morgues, bodies often went unburied for over two days. Dr. Munir criticized the sluggish international response, recalling an instance when the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) sent a commercial fish refrigerator to store dead bodies. Desecration and mutilation of dead bodies Stray dogs mauling unburied corpses became a tragic reality that Dr. Munir cannot forget. He recounted that one hour before Israeli forces stormed Kamal Adwan Hospital, staff had gathered the bodies of 80 victims near the entrance for burial alongside severely wounded patients awaiting transfer. However, an Israeli D9 bulldozer assaulted the area, scooping up both the dead and the wounded together and burying them in a deep pit. Unidentified remains Due to the lack of DNA testing kits from international agencies, countless bodies – many bearing marks of mutilation or having been crushed by tank tracks and bulldozers – could not be identified. When ambulances were unavailable, hospital staff had to pay donkey-cart drivers $5 per body to transport the dead to makeshift burial sites in the market of Jabalia refugee camp. Ultimately, Dr. al-Bursh argued that the atrocities in Gaza surpass standard legal definitions of genocide. “The international community has branded this a genocide by comparing it to crimes committed elsewhere,” he concluded. “From my perspective, what is happening in Gaza aligns with what the Quran describes as the total extermination of production and reproduction.”

articles.title: Anti-austerity protests continue with force in France
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Half a million people took part in demonstrations across France on Tuesday, November 17, in response to a strike call by public sector workers. Tuesday’s strike and protests marked the continuation of a mobilization wave that has shaken the country for approximately two months. “Today was the eleventh round of demonstrations since September 29,” wrote the General Confederation of Labor (CGT). “All in all, in two months, over 5 million demonstrators joined the mobilization for our public services and against the cost of living crisis.” Watch: France’s protest movement is fighting more than Macron “Workers continue to demonstrate their rejection of austerity policies, the deterioration of public services and the erosion of purchasing power,” echoed the trade union organization Solidaires . “Sébastien Lecornu’s announcements at Matignon reinforced the anger and determination to achieve our demands. Meanwhile, the salaries of big bosses are soaring!” Workers say crumbs proposed by government are an affront While the scale of mobilizations over the past weeks appears to have dented the government’s stance, trade unions emphasize that the measures ministers are bringing to the table are far from enough. “The crumbs proposed by David Amiel and Sébastien Lecornu are an affront,” two Solidaires activists said during Tuesday’s protests. “Five-euro pay raises – barely enough to buy a couple more baguettes each month. Public sector workers numbering in the hundreds of thousands stuck below the minimum wage. And an index point for calculating pay that remains frozen.” “Half a million people who took to the streets today prove it – our anger continues to grow, and real solutions need to come to the table.” Students continue to march with trade unions High school and university students once again joined the unions’ mobilization call, reiterating the links between workers’ demands for salary increases and their own demands for more investment in public education and infrastructure, the abolition of the recruitment platform Parcoursup, and more university placements. Read more: Students in France are fighting for stronger public education Echoing workers refusing the crumbs offered by the Lecornu administration while management and shareholder income continues to rise, students insisted they would keep fighting until their full list of demands was met. “We’re not asking for the moon, just the bare minimum for education,” wrote the high school student union Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL). “Our determination is not waning, quite the contrary,” they said . “It’s time to get a political response adequate to our demands.” Mobilizations to continue throughout November Ahead of the most recent day of action, high school and university students once again faced attempts to prevent their mobilization. In Paris, authorities announced that “unannounced actions” – meaning student blockades – would be banned. Police forces could be seen in Nelson Mandela High School in Nantes on November 16 during education minister’s Édouard Geffray visit. Photo: Union Étudiante/Instagram The measure, however, was quickly struck down in administrative court – and students are already preparing for new mobilizations over the weekend. “Many new steps have already been announced,” the CGT wrote. “Thursday, November 19, a national demonstration of retirees; Friday, November 20, with the youth’s call for a European day of action; Saturday, November 21, with a day of mobilization against the cost of living crisis; and Saturday, November 28, with the international day of action for the elimination of gender-based violence.”

articles.title: Why I joined Tempest
articles.author: Keegan O'Brien
articles.content: I’ m writing this message from Belfast, Northern Ireland. I’m on a solo trip around the country, and it’s been absolutely stunning. If you haven’t been to Ireland, I highly recommend making the trip! Today, I visited the James Connolly Museum, and the experience moved me to share some photos and brief reflections about my political life. These past seven-plus years since the dissolution of the International Socialist Organization have been a politically challenging time for me as a revolutionary socialist, as I know they have been for many others. At times, I still feel like I’ve lost my political home and anchor, struggling to stay afloat, make sense of what’s happening in the world, and figure out what comes next. In spite of that, I’m incredibly grateful to be part of the Tempest Collective and to be committed to carrying forward the tradition of revolutionary socialism from below with all of you. My convictions in the politics of working-class self-emancipation, anti-imperialism, international solidarity, the struggle against oppression, and the need for revolutionary organization remain firmer today than at any point in my political life. Like many comrades, I have questions about what the future holds and where we go from here. But I’m proud to be part of an organization where we can figure that out together. We stand on the shoulders of giants and come from a living, breathing political tradition built through the sacrifice and dedication of countless people over decades and centuries. Walking through the museum today and touring the murals throughout the city reminded me that our project is so much greater than any one person or organization. We stand on the shoulders of giants and come from a living, breathing political tradition built through the sacrifice and dedication of countless people over decades and centuries—people who have struggled for a socialist future free of oppression and exploitation, often under circumstances far more grim and difficult than those we face today. It is a tradition built by generations of dedicated revolutionaries who refused to accept the limitations of what was considered possible, and who remained committed to the possibility of a society radically different from the one they inherited. James Connolly’s life and politics are a powerful example of that tradition: They are rooted in working-class self-emancipation, internationalism, anti-imperialism, and the conviction that the liberation of the working class could not be separated from the liberation of the oppressed. Mural in Belfast depicting solidarity between Irish and Palestinian prisoners of war. Image credit: author. After decades of neoliberalism, characterized by working-class retreat and the decline of Left and socialist organizations, it has been inspiring and hopeful to see new generations of people radicalize against the brutality of capitalism and become open to the basic ideas of socialism and working-class politics. In many ways, it is easier today to be a socialist than at any point in my political life. At the same time, being a revolutionary socialist can still be profoundly isolating and difficult, making it easy to question: What am I doing here? Is all our time and effort in this project really worth it? Much of what remains of the socialist Left in the U.S. has either lost sight of or rejected a project of revolutionary transformation. Being part of Tempest reminds me that there are still many of us, albeit a minority, who have refused to let go of that vision. The growth and electoral success of DSA is inspiring and hopeful, but it does not overcome the structural barriers of an electoral road to socialism. Nor does electoral success, by itself, fundamentally alter the balance of class forces or necessarily rebuild the self-organization, political consciousness, and combativity of our class—which we know are the basis for a socialist future. The work we are doing in Tempest, alongside the efforts of comrades and organizations across the revolutionary Left …is part of that longer history and contributes to the ongoing process of reconstituting and rebuilding a rich and vibrant revolutionary movement. Walking around the streets of Belfast today, seeing the incredible murals painted throughout the city, and learning about the life of James Connolly has reminded me that nothing in this world stays fixed forever. Our movements, and this tradition of revolutionary socialism, have gone through many ebbs and flows—periods of tremendous success followed by bleak and difficult setbacks. The work we are doing in Tempest, alongside the efforts of comrades and organizations across the revolutionary Left to develop working-class cadre, advance Marxism as a distinct ideological and political current for understanding and transforming the world, and to rebuild the broader infrastructures of dissent and resistance, is part of that longer history and contributes to the ongoing process of reconstituting and rebuilding a rich and vibrant revolutionary movement, however modest or small these efforts may feel today. We may not see the fruits of that work immediately, or even in our own lifetimes, but by rebuilding this tradition today, we are planting the seeds for the struggles and victories of tomorrow. Mural in Belfast for the Workers Party. Image credit: author. Connolly understood this too, and in his 1909 pamphlet Socialism Made Easy , he captures the revolutionary conviction that what seems impractical in one historical conjuncture may become possible in another—and that our task is to prepare for that moment, even when the balance of class forces and capitalism’s efforts to narrow the collective horizons of our class make the prospects for revolutionary change seem remote: Revolution is never practical—until the hour of the Revolution strikes. Then it alone is practical, and all the efforts of the conservatives and compromisers become the most futile and visionary of human imaginings. For that hour let us work, think and hope; for that hour let us pawn our present ease in hopes of a glorious redemption; for that hour let us prepare the hosts of labor with intelligence sufficient to laugh at the nostrums dubbed practical by our slave-lords, practical for the perpetuation of our slavery; for that supreme crisis of human history, let us watch, like sentinels, with weapons ever ready, remembering always that there can be no dignity in Labor until Labor knows no master. I’m grateful to be on this journey with all of you, fighting for a world where, in Connolly’s words, labor knows no master. Being part of the socialist movement has helped make this life one worth living. We still have a world to win, and I’m committed to fighting for it alongside you. In comradeship and solidarity, Keegan Opinions expressed in signed articles do not necessarily represent the views of the editors or the Tempest Collective. For more information, see “ About Tempest Collective .” Featured Image credit: Keegan O’Brien; modified by Tempest. The post Why I joined Tempest appeared first on Tempest .

articles.title: Why are Mexican cartels fighting in Ukraine?
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: The war in Ukraine has become a training ground for Latin America’s drug cartels: An enforcer for one of Brazil’s biggest gangs was arrested in Rio this month after five on the front lines in Europe. Peter Korotaev, independent journalist and author of Events in Ukraine, joins Zoe Alexandra to unpack why Colombian ex-soldiers, Mexican cartel members and members of a Pentecostal Brazilian gang wound up among the foreign mercenaries fighting Russian forces. Some serve in units tied to HUR, Ukraine’s CIA-trained military intelligence agency, and to the far-right Azov movement, whose longtime leader Serhiy Korotkikh openly follows narco folk saint Santa Muerte. And as cartel drone attacks surge from Mexico to Brazil, Korotaev argues, the violence gives Washington the pretext it needs for further US military intervention in Latin America. Inside Ukraine, Korotaev lays out a forced conscription crisis that has turned the public against Zelensky’s draft, from street roundups by recruitment officers to an Azov detention site outside Kyiv, where soldiers were allegedly beaten and protesters who gathered outside arrested. He breaks down the corruption scandal tying top Ukrainian law enforcement officials to a multibillion-dollar scam call center industry, one he says the European press keeps buried to protect Zelensky. And he explains why Europe, not Moscow or Washington, may be the biggest obstacle to a peace deal in Abu Dhabi. Cartel recruits, CIA-trained spies and a NATO-backed war machine built on systemic corruption: This is the Ukraine story the corporate media won’t report. Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! ****** Rough transcript follows: [Host:] It has been more than four and a half years since the start of the war in Ukraine, and there are strong signs that diplomacy is starting up again. Earlier this month, Russian and Ukrainian negotiators met face to face in Abu Dhabi for the first time in nine months, with the United States mediating. Yet, as we’ve seen in the past week, attacks have continued in Ukrainian and Russian territory. Today, Russian President Vladimir Putin is in China, and he met with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. These are very important talks. We know that the war in Ukraine was not on the agenda. However, it is inevitable that what happens in China these next few days, all of the bilateral talks will have some significant impact. At the same time, there have been significant updates on the ground within Ukraine. To make sense of it all and tell us about these updates within Ukraine, we are joined by Peter Cororov, an independent journalist who is the author of the Substack “Events in Ukraine,” an incredible blog which I hope you all bookmark and subscribe to. Peter, thank you so much and welcome to the show. [Peter Cororov:] Thanks so much for having me. I’m really excited to talk about today. Well, you’ve been following what’s been happening in Ukraine very closely. Before we get into some of the more granular details of these different corruption schemes, foreign mercenaries, etc., I just want to give our viewers a brief overview of the battlefield situation right now. In this moment, could we say that either side has a strategic advantage? And what is the general sentiment that you’re perceiving with regards to peace talks at the moment? [Host:] This year has been interesting on the battlefield because Ukraine has mounted a number of different offensive operations. This has obviously gotten a lot of attention in the western press. It’s important for Ukraine to show that it still has these offensive capacities. But the big question is, of course, what results that gets and also how much Ukraine’s demographic capacities can really handle these offensive operations, which obviously result in plenty of casualties as the war does in general. The offensives haven’t really led to any significant results. There’s lots of debate over which sort of farmland area is under control of Ukraine or Russia, but Ukraine hasn’t managed to take any significant towns. So it’s kind of fighting over this farmland area with little strategic importance. Russia has moved forward slightly in some places. It’s taken most of these two relatively large towns, Toilia and Constant, but it hasn’t been a huge year of military victories on either side. Both governments consider themselves able to weather it out for a significant time longer. The Ukrainians have the Europeans funding them significant amounts. I think the Europeans just passed another 45 billion euros recently. So I don’t really have very high hopes for the negotiations, honestly. Ultimately, the demands on either side are still incommensurable. There’s not much chance, I don’t think. I think it’s mainly Trump has some kind of interest, largely domestic political interest, but I don’t think he really has the real willpower to force Ukraine to accept Russian demands. Even if he did, the Europeans are still there to continue aiding the Ukrainian military. That’s how I see it essentially at the moment. [Peter Cororov:] I don’t know if you saw earlier this morning, Hillary Clinton penned a wild opinion piece essentially criticizing Trump for having met with Vladimir Putin in China and saying, “This is what I would have said to Vladimir Putin if I was there.” Completely out of touch. She’s allegedly a top Democrat and somehow her main focus is why we’re not going to war on the side of Ukraine. Pretty crazy stuff there. But a very interesting element of the war has been the international character that the Ukrainian side has taken on. Beyond the amount of funding from European allies and the United States, the weapons, the political and diplomatic backing, we’re also talking about tens of thousands of foreign mercenaries fighting on behalf of Ukraine. Recently, reports have revealed that members of Mexican drug cartels, Colombian paramilitary groups, etc., are actually on the ground in Ukraine. You wrote about this in a recent piece on Substack called “Narotist.” You highlighted that of all the drone attacks in Latin America since 2018, 72% took place in 2025. This is very astounding. You argue that US support to Ukraine in its war with Russia in terms of intelligence training, weapons supply, etc., is not just about fighting Russia but is also about the US war on the global south. Explain this argument to our viewers. How is it that so many mercenaries, cartel members, and gang members are in Ukraine, and what role does the battlefield in Ukraine play vis-à-vis Washington’s agenda in the global south right now? [Host:] It’s a very interesting story. When I was researching that article, just recently this week, there’s a really remarkable story out of Brazil. I think the Brazilian story kind of encapsulates my broader argument about this and the broader tendencies you can see in Latin America. The majority of the Latin American volunteers are from Colombia. The latest Ukrainian estimates are 7,000 Colombians fighting for Ukraine, a total of 16,000 foreign volunteers. Then, a few thousand different Ecuadorians, Mexicans, and plenty of Brazilians. The Brazil story is very interesting. Basically, on the 12th of November, the Brazilian press reported on the arrest in Rio of a certain individual with the street name Predator. He’s a 26-year-old who spent five months fighting in Ukraine. He is a member of the Tercero Commando Puro (TCP) cartel. He was arrested for being a member of this cartel and was in charge of the security apparatus. It’s very interesting if you look at the actual nature of this cartel. TCP is the third largest cartel in Brazil. It’s actually a Pentecostal cartel. This is the phenomenon of narco-Pentecostalism in Brazil, where Pentecostalism, of American origin, is very right-wing, very opposed to Lula, and very aligned with the Bolsonaro movement. They are very pro-American, obviously. Cartels, as a business group that thrives off of exploiting the poor, have some sort of organic relationship or tendency for them to be interested in ideas of Pentecostalism and the idea that the state shouldn’t exist. This cartel, for instance, considers the state to be like Satan, and they need to fight against it. They are also very pro-Israel. They have a huge Star of David hanging in the neighborhoods they control in Rio, and they have flags of Israel everywhere. They are quite friendly with the police as far as cartels go, which is interesting considering the general right-wing tendency of police forces in Latin America. It’s very interesting that of all the cartels, the one that has been at least arrested for going to Ukraine is in this cartel. I think you can make the argument really if you look at the broader function of the cartels in Latin America. For instance, in Ecuador in 2024, there was this supposed cartel uprising. The right-wing president of Ecuador used this very well to declare a state of war and invited more US military presence within the country. It’s kind of a playbook all around Latin America. El Salvador is a similar case. Mexico still has a left-wing government, and there was also this strange case at the beginning of this year with an almost cartel uprising when the Mexican government assassinated or captured El Mencho, the head of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). There was an uprising against the government. The American right-wing press was amplifying this, trying to portray Mexico’s government as collapsing. Laura Loomer said that Sheinbaum had been evacuated, and the press secretary of the White House said military action is necessary if American citizens are threatened. Very much an attempt to use cartel instability as an excuse for US military intervention into this left-wing government, which Trump is not very happy with, and in general, most US administrations are not very happy with. The reason I bring up the name of the cartel is because there was a famous video in October from Al Jazeera on the topic of Latin American foreign fighters in Ukraine. There were about ten Latin Americans, and they said they had come back from missions in Ecuador, Colombia, and Mexico. At least one of them introduced himself as being from the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, which is quite striking. You can really see an interesting tendency. In terms of the way that these Latin Americans serve in the Ukrainian army, it’s often very close to the Ukrainian military intelligence apparatus. They serve in all units of the Ukrainian army, but they often tend to have special units just for them for language purposes. One particularly interesting example is a unit called the Advanced Company Unit, which has about 100-150 members. It’s part of Ukrainian military intelligence (GUR), which is the Ukrainian intelligence agency trained most by the CIA and MI6. There’s plenty in the western press about it. This unit, Advanced Company Unit, is led by a Brazilian gentleman named Le Anderson Paulino. He has a large Instagram profile and tries to accentuate how criminal he looks. There was a scandal at the start of this year where he beat one of his subordinates to death, with systematic torture and sexual abuse of recruits in this unit. It was covered by the Ukrainian western-funded press. You look at the members of this unit, and they look fairly unsavory. There’s probably strong evidence that this fellow in the Pentecostal cartel might have served in this unit because this is essentially a unit of Brazilian mercenaries in Ukraine. The Brazilian press talks about how it was some sort of military intelligence training unit. The GUR Ukrainian military intelligence, where this unit of Brazilian fighters is, is renowned for having their operators around the world. For instance, in the Sahel, training separatists. In September, the former head of the GUR, Budanov, who’s now Zelensky’s chief of staff, posted photographs of GUR operatives in Mali, which was quite something because until then, the Ukrainian foreign ministry had always denied any involvement. He proudly posted these photographs in Mali training Tuareg fighters. CNN has also written about it, how the Ukrainians have systematically trained them in the use of drones as drone operators. There’s a remarkable article I’m going to write about this week in the Ukrainian press, which claimed that Ukraine’s GUR operatives in Sudan were on the side of rebels fighting against General Al-Burhan, who is pro-Russian, which would mean the RSF, obviously, which is a remarkable statement to make. All that is said is that these GUR operatives have this existing tendency towards training US-aligned forces around the world. There are some cases in Congo, possibly to do with Rwanda. The final thing I would say is that there’s a recent book by Wall Street Journal correspondent Bojan Pancevski. He’s a pro-journalist. It’s about Nord Stream, but that’s not important. It has an interesting section in it when it talks about a 2017 training course that took place in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and in the US. It was curated by the CIA and Dutch intelligence, and then in the US, obviously just the CIA. It was for Ukrainian intelligence operatives to conduct covert work in foreign countries. According to Pancevski, who’s very pro-Ukrainian and pro-NATO, the aim was for them to be used in contexts conducive to US interests. He gave the example of Cuba and Mexico, which is quite interesting. There’s no evidence of any Ukrainian citizens or operatives in Latin America. But it is interesting that you have these cartel members from Latin America fighting in these Ukrainian intelligence agency units, getting drone training, and going back and then using this drone training in ways that are arguably fairly conducive to US foreign policy goals. [Peter Cororov:] It’s really harrowing, especially when you see the front lines of the anti-imperialist struggle being in the Sahel. This new imperialist onslaught against Latin America and this connection with Ukraine is quite concerning. I did want you to just dig in a bit more to the frequency of these drone strikes happening in 2025. Essentially, people are going to Ukraine, learning how to use these drones, and coming back. Where is this happening? You also wrote about Sergey Kurotikk, an influential figure in the Azov movement in the Ukrainian army. You said he is a follower of Santa Muerte and was even in Ecuador where he found these ideas. To add to this narrative, who is this figure and how are people like him playing a role in the recruitment of these far-right mercenaries? What does it say about the ideological character of this battlefield and the fight against Russia? [Host:] There’s an interesting statistic that last year alone, there were 34,000 drone flights detected by US law enforcement on the border with Mexico. The Mexican side even had a case recently where American law enforcement used a laser system to shoot down three drones near Texas, apparently controlled by Mexican cartels. There have been numerous cases as well. In October, there was a drone attack on the state attorney’s general’s office in Tijuana by cartels. They attacked the kidnapping units. There was also a raid in Sinaloa where they found 15 FPV drones and different specialized equipment. In Brazil, late last year, an anti-drone system that jams and shoots them down was discovered in a raid on a Brazilian cartel. The drone system had a Ukrainian nationalist trident on it, and it was written in English. The Brazilian press reported on it and got the opinion of some Ukrainian expert who said it might not be Ukrainian. The American expert community, like the CSIS based in Washington, has been writing about how cartels have used drones for a long time, long before the Ukraine war. But what’s difficult is actually operating the drones. It’s quite difficult to learn how to operate these drones, and the skills acquired on the battlefield in Ukraine are very useful. This is why Ukrainian drone operators have been going across the world to the Gulf to help the UAE and whatnot. It’s easy to buy drones, but actually having the skills to operate them is very different. Without training, you’re likely to fail navigating complex environments. There is definitely a strategy on the side of organized crime to send their operatives there. Ideologically, the majority of Colombians who go, it’s about 7,000 apparently fighting, is the largest Latin American group. They’re largely veterans of the armed forces or different other law enforcement units. Often in coverage of this, there’s a somewhat depoliticized view of it. They’re going for salary, which I’m sure is true to some extent as well. There’s an article by Ukrainian state media mentioning how the Colombians are fighting in Ukraine for the cause of freedom, but it also mentions how their experience fighting against guerillas back in Colombia has been very helpful for them. This is an interesting admission because the Colombian army law enforcement was forged fighting against left-wing guerrillas against FARC and so on, and also engaged in various massacres of peasant communities and often aligned with different right-wing paramilitaries that are essentially drug cartels. There are definitely ideological reasons why they might go to Ukraine, which also has this pervasive right-wing ideology, anti-communism. There’s an interesting Azov Ukrainian nationalist telegram channel with about 20,000 followers called Tales of the Fourth Empire. In 2019, there’s an interesting post where it talks about the campaign of murders of former FARC members in Colombia, and the author was very happy about this. He said that Ukraine should use a similar approach if we have a political settlement with the East Ukrainian pro-Russian separatists. They see it as a similar fight because anti-communism, anti-left-wing ideology is the main ideology of Azov. It makes sense why they would be aligned in that sense. There are obviously some Colombians that have gone to fight on the Russian side, but according to the estimates by the Ukrainians, it’s significantly less, about half less for the Russians than for the Ukrainians. There are all kinds. The last thing about Kurotikk, he’s a very interesting figure. There are rumors that before he was actually of Russian descent, but he was the second most important figure in the Azov movement from its founding until 2022. He’s sort of in the shadows now, but he’s very influential in the assault units, which are very famous and brutal units that have had many scandals in Ukrainian press because of systematic torture and execution of deserters. Kurotikk was one of the leaders of this group of units, which has about 20-30,000 troops in it. It still exists, although it’s been somewhat reformed supposedly. In 2019-2020, he said that he’s a big fan of Santa Muerte, which is a semi-religion of certain Latin American organized crime groups. It’s somewhat of a religion of death, some sort of satanic or something. He’s into it, and different satanic pagan beliefs are very popular in the post-Soviet white nationalist scene. He’s definitely an important figure in recruiting for these different units. He’s still very close to the assault units, and the assault units are actually very closely aligned with this Brazilian cartel group that I mentioned recently, the Advanced Company Unit. It’s part of this larger unit called Revenge, which is obviously a right-wing name, and they’re very right-wing. They’re neo-Nazis. You look in the telegram channels, and they’re always posting all this kind of stuff. They made a collection called the Christian Core two months ago, a collection of different units, and you have people from the assault units who come with organized crime background who are part of this collection and advertise themselves as being right-wing Christian nationalists. There’s a figure there, Kachinsky, who famously said that he wants there to be a Christian Taliban in Ukraine. He’s a bit of a comical figure, but also he’s in charge of a military unit, and he’s always calling to kill deserters on TV. There’s an ecosystem of these very right-wing figures in the Ukrainian army, many with organized crime links. Kurotikk, this Santa Muerte guy, is renowned for being an organized criminal. In the 2000s, when he was in Russia, he was part of a big murderous neo-Nazi group that killed dozens of migrants. He somehow escaped, but it was found that his bank account had 200 million rubles. He’s a very strange individual in Ukraine. He has a plane for some reason, a private plane. These are all figures that clearly have international connections, organized crime connections, and quite high-level positions in Europe’s largest army now. [Peter Cororov:] I know we’re going on here, but I do want to get your perspective on a couple more things. A couple of weeks ago, there was a lot of news about a secret detention center that was allegedly discovered. There were draft dodgers and deserters tortured and beaten. But then there was a strong pushback from mainstream media and Ukrainian politicians that this was all fabricated and somehow a Russian plot. Your thoughts on this? What really happened here? Beyond this specific media incident, what is the situation with regards to deserters and the general sentiment towards service right now? [Host:] There was an interesting video by a medic from the Azov. It was from the third corps, but basically the major Azov military unit. She complained on television that she went to a school and saw that school children don’t know anything about NATO. They don’t care about NATO, but they care a lot about these abuses by the mobilization forces called the TRC, territorial recruitment centers, which have become massively hated in Ukrainian society. She was very sad about this. She says there needs to be a re-education of the youth. Apparently, they don’t know anything about Azov’s main military operations. That’s just an example of how distant the nationalist elite is from the people, the majority of people that really don’t care about this massively bloody war, but they do care about when their relatives are dragged off the street, kicking and screaming, and sent into a bus, and they die within a few weeks. With this case in a suburb of Kiev, the whole media response of denying anything bad happened is quite funny because if you look at the Ukrainian press, every day there’s a new case of torture, extortion, deaths in the Ukrainian army, in the mobilization structures, the TRC. These are not reports by random people. These are criminal cases launched by Ukraine’s law enforcement agencies against individual representatives of the TRC. It’s totally systematic. There was a remarkable estimate by one Ukrainian MP that the amount of bribes each year is two billion euros. It’s huge in terms of getting out of the mobilization process. At every single step of the way, there’s someone you can pay a bribe to, and if you don’t pay the bribe, you get beaten. Ultimately, you’ll get sent to the front where you will likely die. There are endless schemes of how to pay this money, who to pay, huge business. Beatings are an essential part of it because it makes you more likely to pay. It’s also a way to discipline soldiers because these are civilians, they don’t really want to fight, and they need to be somehow disciplined into going into a battle where they will likely die. The point being is that this claim that nothing happened there, maybe there were some aspects because it became a very viral event in Kiev where many people got very excited and angry, and some of them had relatives stuck in there. There might have been some exaggerations. There was some report someone died there, we don’t know, but the thing is we don’t know. Maybe someone did die, but then last week, a week after this event, the military ombudsman, Ukraine’s military ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said that there probably were beatings in this place. The head of Ukraine’s chief of staff, Budanov, said when he went there to save the people from there that there are thousands of sites like this. This site was a temporary holding site where they keep soldiers that have violated discipline in some way. Some of them tried to desert, some of them may have been caught drinking or whatnot. Maybe some of them didn’t pay extortion fees, which are very common in the Ukrainian army as well, and they were kept there. We know from the photos that some of them were beaten. They had black eyes. The medical reports showed that there was one person there who had a stoma, so he had his stomach open. He basically went to the toilet through this tube and was just left there in this hole in the ground. He was getting an infection, disgusting abscess, and so on. These were terrible conditions. In the weeks since, there’s been no real investigation of the military. This was a military, it was Azov, it was the first national guard corps and first Azov corps, and they were the ones in charge of this place. There’s been no investigation into them, but there have been about 20 people arrested, protesters who protested outside of this building. They’ve been arrested and face 5 to 8 years in jail, very serious sentences for obstructing military personnel. These were just ordinary people, mainly young people. They were sent to jail for two months without any possibility of bail, which is quite a big contrast to these huge corruption cases in Ukraine where the ministers and people in Zelensky’s orbit sometimes get charged but with the possibility of bail, so they just pay the bail and leave quite early. This happens very regularly, whereas ordinary people obviously don’t have this option. There have been quite a few of these protests this year against mobilization. In June or July, there was a large protest in Lviv, which is a western city known for being very nationalist. People there are very angry about mobilization as well. There was a large protest of mainly youth against the mobilization authorities, and the police scared them away eventually. They managed to free some person from the mobilization, and then in the weeks later, the nationalists, Azov, captured these youth. They forced them to apologize on camera. One person had been visibly very severely beaten or tortured. He was crying and giving this apology, and he was going to be sent to the army. This is a video that was posted proudly by Azov people who call to kill all draft dodgers. They’re all cowards. The video is harrowing. The guy is an adult, in his mid-20s, looks like a guy from the streets, not a sensitive guy, and he’s barely able to say anything. Something really terrible was done to him. That’s what happens. [Peter Cororov:] Really harrowing stuff. One last thing I wanted to hear from you about is this corruption scandal in Ukraine with regards to the Himrom cartel and its dealings in drug trafficking and call center mafia. Briefly give us an overview of what’s happening with this scandal. What role does this cartel play in Ukrainian politics? What does it say about the Zelensky government and this so-called defense of freedom and democracy that Europe and the Democratic Party in the US are so eager to join and support? [Host:] This is a pretty remarkable story. On a diplomatic level, this organized crime group called Himrom, its leader currently lives in Mexico. It’s just one group of scam call centers. It controlled about 50 scam call centers. There was a peak of about 1,500 scam call centers. In total, these scam call centers, according to European Swiss organized crime investigators, generated 12 billion dollars a year, which is huge numbers. 85% of their victims were not Russian but European. The propaganda line in Ukraine always was these scam call centers are fine because they only scam Russian grandmothers, which often causes suicides. These are very sadistic people. They have TikToks, and they talk about it, very proud of it, and share their funniest stories of when some pensioner said they’re going to commit suicide or whatever because they scammed them out of everything, and they revel in this. Even the scam call center cartel person said that probably the scam call centers are evil because of the damage done to the employees, the psychological damage. According to the Swiss press, they employed about 100,000 people, which is remarkable, a huge amount of people. There are very few jobs in Ukraine nowadays. You’ll often see advertisements for these scam call centers. The Russian government managed to crack down on them fairly well, and now for the past few years, they’ve really been targeting Europeans. According to this head of Himrom, there’s even specialized scam call centers that target only America, only the United States. According to him, the head of Himrom, he says that the scam call centers generated $20 billion a year for Ukraine, not 12 billion like the Swiss, which is entirely possible. Ukrainian law enforcement, this is the European-funded section of Ukrainian law enforcement, released transcripts of wiretap conversations showing the head of Himrom talking with top figures in Ukraine’s intelligence agencies, law enforcement agencies about the rent they would get. Burkin said, “Yes, it’s all true.” Each scam call center would pay $21,000 US each month to the big three law enforcement agencies: the security services, the national police, and the general prosecutor. Last month, Ukraine’s general prosecutor, technically the most powerful law enforcement figure in the country, fled to Austria because of this whole investigation into his curation of these scam call centers and his profiting off these scam call centers. This is a figure close with Zelensky, known for being very loyal to Zelensky. The same is true for the National Police and Services. They’ve all been identified as being involved with these scam call centers. If you add up the number of bribes they were getting, the Himrom leader says it added up to $370 million US a year just in bribes to the Ukrainian government to keep these scam call centers open. If you don’t pay the bribes, they would raid the scam call center, close it down, and so on. The last interesting thing about this is that there’s been nothing in the western press about this. Before last year, Zelensky tried to close down the anti-corruption agencies that the western countries had set up to control the Ukrainian government in a sense. When Zelensky tried to shut them down, there was lots in the western press about Zelensky abandoning democracy. It’s very bad. Zelensky backed down and let them be. These anti-corruption agencies are very pro-NATO, very supportive of continuing the war. But now there’s nothing about this huge scandal of the Ukrainian government curating scams targeting European citizens in the European press. This is information revealed by law enforcement agencies that Europe created and sponsors and protects. It’s not a Russian psy-op or whatever. I think it’s because there are negotiations right now. The Europeans don’t want to damage Zelensky’s position. They want him to continue the war. If they damage his image, there could be more dissent in Europe about whether this is a government that should be supported with billions of dollars. The fact that the European press hasn’t covered it at all is a testament to this. This is also why I don’t really believe that much in these negotiations, unfortunately, because the Europeans seem very intent on the Ukraine project. [Peter Cororov:] Yeah, and as if it weren’t costing billions of dollars and more importantly tens of thousands of lives. Peter, thank you so much for joining us and really digging into all of these different elements. I know it was a lot, but there’s just so much to discuss. You are the only person who can read not only the Ukrainian press and tell us what’s happening on the ground but provide excellent analysis. Thank you so much for joining us here at BT Live. [Peter Cororov:] Thanks so much.

articles.title: A Great Reversal: Washington and Caracas sign new military agreement
articles.author: Manolo De los Santos
articles.content: On November 18, 2026, acting President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, presided over the signing by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Venezuelan Minister of Defense Gustavo González López of a military cooperation agreement in Caracas. Speaking from the US Embassy in Caracas, Hegseth arrogantly stated that Venezuela “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.” Rubbing salt in the wound, Hegseth boasted that his trip was only “made possible” by the January 3rd operation that kidnapped President Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores, and left 32 Cubans and over 100 Venezuelans dead. This he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America,” which “solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours.” He recounted that “exactly one year ago today” Maduro “stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth added, “Well, we answered that call,” calling Maduro and Flores “narco-terrorists.” The accord, announced during an unannounced visit, provides for the resumption of technical and military cooperation, including joint training, intelligence sharing, and access to new equipment and technologies for Venezuela’s armed forces. For Washington, it marks the return of a military relationship that had been interrupted for twenty-one years by the Bolivarian Revolution. For Venezuela, it represents a definitive close to the “anti-imperialist phase” articulated by Hugo Chávez in 2004-2005, and a de facto alignment with Trump’s project to renew total US control over Latin America and the Caribbean. All countries of the region now have military agreements with Washington, with the exception of Cuba and Nicaragua. The significance of the signing cannot be understood without the historical record that preceded it. The function of US military cooperation US military cooperation with Venezuela has never been a neutral technical exchange. US military training shaped the officer corps that carried out state repression against Venezuela’s left for decades. During the 1950s, Washington backed the dictatorship of Marcos Pérez Jiménez, whose government was notorious for its brutality and whose security forces were trained and equipped by the United States. Later, the US Army’s School of the Americas trained thousands of Latin American officers, including Venezuelans, in counterinsurgency tactics, including interrogation, torture, and summary execution, and since the 1960s, the successive governments of the corrupt 4th Republic had been deploying those methods against the Communist Party and other left organizations, with the national police agency DIGEPOL responsible for extensive human rights abuses. That same institutional lineage was on display in the February 1989 Caracazo, a mass popular uprising against IMF austerity measures, when the US-trained military was ordered to restore order, and hundreds of civilians were killed; as Chávez, himself a military officer, later said, the massacre “created consciousness among many military personnel, especially the younger ones,” and the officers who witnessed and carried out the repression were products of a system long tutored by the United States. The Caracazo became the breaking point that convinced Chávez and his co-conspirators in the MBR-200 movement that they “could not continue to defend a murderous regime,” setting in motion the February 4, 1992 rebellion. Declassified Pentagon training manuals endorsed torture, extortion, and execution, and several Venezuelan generals who later participated in the 2002 coup against Chávez were graduates of the School of the Americas. This was not an aberration but a consistent feature of a security relationship designed to align Latin American militaries with Washington’s Cold War in a counterinsurgency strategy in which close to 200,000 people are estimated to have been forcibly disappeared for their left-wing political activism. The most personal and politically charged example of this history is the 1976 torture and murder of Jorge Antonio Rodríguez, father of Delcy Rodríguez. Rodríguez, a socialist activist and leader of the Socialist League, was detained by Venezuela’s DISIP intelligence service and died in custody after what his family and numerous accounts describe as torture. As Craig Murray noted in Consortium News, the killing occurred at the hands of “the CIA-backed security services of the US-aligned [Carlos Andrés] Pérez regime”. That his daughter, now the acting president, would preside over such a military accord is a measure of the transformation imposed by the US on Venezuela’s political leadership since January 3rd. Military transformation was key to the Bolivarian Revolution’s radicalism In April 2005, on his program Aló Presidente, Chávez announced the indefinite suspension of all military exchanges with the United States. He stated that US military advisers stationed in Venezuelan bases had been “waging a campaign” among the Venezuelan military against his government and the Bolivarian Revolution. “All exchanges with US officers are suspended until who knows when,” he said. “There will be no more combined operations, nothing like that”. Chávez’s decision was a direct response to growing US hostility to the Bolivarian Revolution. In addition to the 2002 coup attempt against him, which senior US officials were closely linked to, US agencies provided continued funding of opposition groups, and cover for intelligence operations against the government. The suspension was an assertion of sovereignty, a refusal to allow a foreign power to maintain a military presence inside the country, while seeking to overthrow and undermine the constitutional order. The expulsion of the US forces was a turning point in the radicalization of the Bolivarian Revolution, and set the stage for the transformation of the state apparatus. After the 2005 suspension of US military exchanges, Venezuela moved decisively to remake its armed forces as a sovereign institution. They purged the officer corps of those tied to the old US-aligned command structure and promoted a new military doctrine to erase the legacy of decades of US military instruction. This transformation tied the military directly to the Bolivarian project. Chávez described the armed forces as being “at the very heart of the revolution,” and the institution was reconceived as a guarantor of the people’s democratic gains and national sovereignty rather than an instrument of external powers. The concept of unión cívico-militar , or the union of the masses and the military, first proposed by Chávez in 1999, became the military’s official doctrine. In a region with a long history of right-wing coups, all other progressive presidents elected in the “pink tide” were constantly looking over their shoulders, worried that their high command remained loyal to their oligarchies. Not so in Venezuela. Having broken the Venezuelan military away from the Pentagon and trained new layers of officers and soldiers in anti-imperialism, the Bolivarian state put down continued coup plots and did not snap under the highest-pressure scenarios. For two decades, Venezuela refused to accept the presence of US military personnel and instead built security relationships with Russia, China, and other partners. But the US never abandoned its objective of regime change. Economic sanctions, diplomatic isolation, and covert action intensified. The decisive action came on January 3, 2026, when US forces conducted a military raid in Caracas, captured President Nicolás Maduro, and transported him to New York. Delcy Rodríguez, previously vice president, was sworn in as acting president. From that moment, Venezuela’s cooperation with the United States began not as a negotiated partnership between sovereign states, but as a relationship shaped by the reality of military threats and political coercion. A different kind of change in course The November 18 agreement formalizes that relationship. Hegseth described it as a “renewal of our defense partnership” and praised Rodríguez for “close cooperation” that allowed officials “to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists”. The language is telling. The agreement’s provisions, training, intelligence sharing, equipment, and technology are precisely the mechanisms through which the United States integrates a subordinate military into its own command and intelligence architecture. There is no suggestion that Venezuela will receive reciprocal access to US decision-making, or that the relationship will be governed by any principle other than Washington’s strategic agenda for total domination in the region. The agreement must be situated within the broader US strategy that has come to be called the “Donroe Doctrine.” The term, a modification of the Monroe Doctrine, describes a renewed US claim to unilateral control over the Western Hemisphere. The doctrine aims to intervene directly in regional affairs, reinforce US military presence in Latin America and the Caribbean, and plunder resources to cut off China from natural resources, critical minerals, and supply chains. The January 2026 operation against Maduro was its first open application. The “Shield of the Americas,” launched in March 2026 , is its institutional vehicle: a US-led multinational security and political alliance ostensibly formed to combat drug cartels, but which in practice commits member states to “the use of lethal military force” and to limiting “foreign geopolitical interference” in the hemisphere. The coalition’s motto, as announced by Hegseth, is “We do bad things to bad people.” Such language is the naked arrogance of US imperialism. Venezuela’s signature on November 18 is therefore not merely a bilateral military agreement. The agreement commits Venezuela’s armed forces to interoperability with the US military, to intelligence sharing that will inevitably flow toward Washington’s regional command structures, and to a training relationship that will shape the doctrine and loyalties of a new generation of Venezuelan officers. In exchange, Venezuela receives equipment and technology. It is normal for even the most revolutionary governments to seek normal, diplomatic and peaceful relations with the great capitalist powers. Existing in a system of states, they may even have mutually beneficial areas of cooperation, while remaining ideological and political adversaries. But that is not the context for this agreement. A government whose president was kidnapped after a foreign military operation, facing continued economic sanctions and the implicit threat of further intervention, cannot be said to have negotiated as a sovereign equal. The history of US military cooperation in Venezuela, from Pérez Jiménez to the School of the Americas to the 2002 coup, demonstrates that Washington’s security relationships in the region have only one purpose: control. There is no military threat posed to the U.S. from any country in Latin America – “mutual defense” in this context is an absurdity and a smokescreen. The November 18 agreement revives the long history of domination and compliance under a new name. It marks a major turn in US-Venezuelan relations, but not toward equality or reconciliation. It formalizes a relationship of subordination, concluded under duress. In that sense, Hegseth did tell the truth about one thing, how he began his remarks: “Just one year ago, my presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.”

articles.title: Senegalese president removed from PASTEF amid budget standoff
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Senegal’s governing party, PASTEF-Les Patriotes, has struck President Bassirou Diomaye Faye off its membership list, formalizing its break with the man it carried to power in March 2024. Two days later, Faye bypassed the party’s parliamentary majority by bringing a rejected budget into force by decree. At a meeting on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, PASTEF’s National Council (Conseil national) removed Faye and 31 others, among them serving ministers. Only releasing a brief communiqué, numbered C N°02/PASTEF/CN/2026: “Pursuant to the provisions of Article 6 of the statutes of PASTEF-LES PATRIOTES, the National Council of the party, at its meeting of Tuesday 17 November 2026, formally noted the automatic loss of membership of PASTEF-LES PATRIOTES of the persons listed below … Accordingly, they are permanently struck off the party’s membership list.” The list includes Yankhoba Diémé, minister of the Armed Forces, who stayed in Faye’s government in June despite the party’s boycott. It also includes Aldiouma Sow, a member of PASTEF’s National Political Bureau and minister-adviser at the Presidency. A partnership that came apart Faye and Ousmane Sonko emerged as a single political project. When Sonko was barred from the 2024 presidential race, he designated Faye, then PASTEF’s secretary-general, as the party’s candidate under the slogan “Diomaye mooy Sonko” (“Diomaye is Sonko”). Faye won in the first round and named Sonko prime minister. The partnership broke down over governance and economic management. On May 22, 2026, Faye dismissed Sonko and dissolved the government, appointing the economist Ahmadou Al Aminou Lo as prime minister. PASTEF refused to join the new cabinet announced on June 1. Read more: Senegal leadership rift escalates as President Faye removes popular Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko Sonko then returned to the National Assembly, where lawmakers elected him speaker. PASTEF holds 130 of the Assembly’s 165 seats, and on June 6 its first ordinary congress re-elected Sonko party president unanimously. Faye, for his part, moved to build his own base. On July 25, 2026, he launched Kiiraay – Les Patriotes Républicains, a party with no seats in the Assembly. Read more: Political rift in Senegal deepens as parliament moves to limit presidential powers A budget brought into force by decree The split now runs through Senegal’s public finances. On November 3, the PASTEF majority rejected the government’s 2026 amending finance law (supplementary budget) in a plenary vote. From November 7, the Assembly’s Finance Committee went on to reject most of the items in the 2027 budget bill. On Thursday, November 19, the presidency answered with a communiqué signed by Oumar Samba Ba, minister and secretary-general of the presidency: “The President of the Republic, guardian of the Constitution and guarantor of the regular functioning of public authorities and of the continuity of the State, has decided to bring into force the draft amending finance law (supplementary budget) for the year 2026 by means of Decree No. 2026-2416 of 19 November 2026.” The communiqué cites no specific constitutional provision for the decree. It covers only the 2026 supplementary budget; the 2027 budget remains stalled in Parliament. The standoff comes as Senegal continues to face debt burdens in Africa. In February 2025, a Court of Auditors report found that borrowing had been under-reported for years under the previous government of Macky Sall. The IMF suspended its program after about $13 billion in undeclared debt came to light, and puts total public-sector debt at about 132% of GDP at the end of 2024. In September 2026, Senegal and the IMF agreed on a program of about $2.2 billion over 36 months, but the Fund’s board has not yet approved it. What happened to the optimism Faye and Sonko rose by mobilizing around mass youth unemployment, the rising cost of living, frustration with neoliberal policies, and anger at the political establishment. Those grievances had fueled years of protest and instability, and the pair’s victory raised hopes, in Senegal and across the continent, for a new kind of leadership. After the separation, Sonko continued to command the grassroots base and kept his grip on the parliamentary majority, while Faye held the presidency. That meant Faye was always likely to face sustained pressure, both from Sonko and PASTEF.
